question: Can the same introduced butterfly larval host be an actual feeding resource for one native butterfly and a lethal oviposition trap for a close relative, despite both links appearing as equally usable in HOSTS?

case.plant_origins: introduced in Florida from South America

data: Fixed HOSTS–WCVP sidecars generated in chocho Actions run 37628559686 plus TTF frozen resource descriptors run 36222306369
predefined_local_calculations: exact native and contemporary potential host resource unions for each butterfly
introduced-only resources uniquely requiring Aristolochia littoralis as a recorded host (excluding its native plant ranges)
exact shared-host butterfly-pair×WGSRPD3 opportunity units that disappear if the B. philenor × A. littoralis edge is disallowed specifically in introduced plant regions
count introduced-plant regions and all known host users in 239 eligible butterflies
important_limit: Fitness contrast published for Florida context, not all 48 introduced WGSRPD3 units. Do not call globally removed opportunities actual traps, colonizations or losses; this is a literature-grounded upper-bound sensitivity example. B. polydamas successful reproductive performance on each introduced region is not established.
ecological_meaning: Potential host breadth and shared-host exposure can have discordant fitness signs even for phylogenetically related butterfly species; raw host-link counts do not measure benefit.
status_of_novelty: Specific case is known in literature; globalization of this asymmetry across 239 butterflies is not established and not claimed. GEB main unchanged.
